title: SIRVALUE: from BASIC to Python
text:
← PreviousSIR model: from BASIC to PythonAll appsNext →Graphing S: from BASIC to Python
This page runs the SIRVALUE program from the BASIC listing below (see page 65), rewritten in Python. The Python runs right here in your browser, and the table shows whatever the program prints. Edit the code and press Run to update it; Reset brings back the original program.
The model is the same as before: susceptible people become infected at a rate of a × S × I, and infected people recover at a rate of b × I, with a = 0.00001 and b = 1 / 14. What’s new is the goal. Instead of printing a value every day, SIRVALUE estimates S, I and R at a single later time, tfinal = 1. It gets there by splitting the interval from tinitial to tfinal into numberofsteps = 10 equal steps, so deltat = (1 - 0) / 10 = 0.1, and taking one Euler step for each.

title: SIRVALUE: from BASIC to Python
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program (SIRVALUE.BAS)





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  tinitial = 0
 3  tfinal = 1
 4  t = tinitial
 5  S = 45400
 6  I = 2100
 7  R = 2500
 8  numberofsteps = 10
 9  deltat = (tfinal - tinitial) / numberofsteps
10  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
11          Sprime = -.00001 * S * I
12          Iprime = .00001 * S * I - I / 14
13          Rprime = I / 14
14          deltaS = Sprime * deltat
15          deltaI = Iprime * deltat
16          deltaR = Rprime * deltat
17          t = t + deltat
18          S = S + deltaS
19          I = I + deltaI
20          R = R + deltaR
21  NEXT k
22  PRINT t, S, I, R

title: Graphing S: from BASIC to Python
text:
← PreviousSIRVALUE: from BASIC to PythonAll appsNext →Graphing S until the peak: a DO-WHILE loop
This page runs a BASIC program that graphs S, the number of susceptible people, over three days. The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The calculation is the same Euler’s method as in SIRVALUE, now with tfinal = 3 and numberofsteps = 30, so deltat = 0.1. The new part is the drawing. On each pass through the loop, LINE (t, S)-(t + deltat, S + deltaS) draws a straight segment from the current point to the next one, and together the 30 segments form a piecewise-linear approximation to the graph of S. WINDOW (0, 40000)-(3, 45400) sets the coordinates of the screen, so t runs from 0 to 3 across and S runs from 40,000 to 45,400 up. (SCREEN 12 just switches the computer into graphics mode.)
In the Python, window(...) and line(...) do the same jobs as WINDOW and LINE. Try setting numberofsteps to 3 to see the individual segments, or to 300 for a smoother curve.

title: Graphing S until the peak: a DO-WHILE loop
text:
← PreviousGraphing S: from BASIC to PythonAll appsNext →A sequence of approximations: nested loops and color
This page runs a BASIC program that graphs S, the number of susceptible people, and keeps going until the epidemic reaches its peak. The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The calculation and the drawing are the same as in SIRPLOT: Euler’s method with deltat = 0.01, and LINE (t, S)-(t + deltat, S + deltaS) drawing one short segment per step. What changes is how the program decides when to stop. SIRPLOT used a FOR loop, so it ran a fixed number of steps. This program doesn’t know ahead of time how many steps it needs. Instead it uses DO WHILE Iprime > 0 ... LOOP, which repeats the loop for as long as the number of infected people is still increasing. When Iprime is no longer positive, I has reached its peak, the loop stops, and PRINT t reports when that happened.
Because the condition is checked at the top of the loop, Iprime has to be given a value before the loop starts, which is why it is calculated once on its own line before DO WHILE. WINDOW (0, 0)-(20, 47000) makes the screen wide and tall enough to hold the whole run: t from 0 to 20 days across and S from 0 to 47,000 up.
In the Python, while Iprime > 0: does the job of DO WHILE, and print(t) does the job of PRINT t; the printed time appears under the graph. You’ll see a long decimal rather than a tidy 12.28, because adding 0.01 over and over builds up tiny rounding errors. Try changing deltat to 0.1 or 0.001 to see how the peak time shifts, or change the 14 in the recovery rate. If you change the model so that Iprime never drops to 0, the loop never ends; the page stops any program that runs longer than five seconds.

title: A sequence of approximations: nested loops and color
text:
← PreviousGraphing S until the peak: a DO-WHILE loopAll appsNext →Arc length: adding up short segments
This page runs a BASIC program that solves the same differential equation fourteen times, each time with twice as many steps as the time before, and draws all fourteen approximations on one graph. The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The equation is the logistic equation
\[
y' = 0.1\, y \left(1 - \frac{y}{1000}\right), \qquad y(0) = 100,
\]
solved with Euler’s method from t = 0 to t = 75. The inner loop, FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps, is Euler’s method itself, the same pattern as SIRPLOT but with one variable instead of three. The outer loop, FOR j = 1 TO 14, runs that whole calculation again and again. Each time through, numberofsteps = 2 ^ (j - 1) doubles the number of steps (1, 2, 4, …, 8192), so deltat is cut in half. The first approximation is a single straight segment; the last one has 8192 segments, each less than a hundredth of a day long. Watching the graphs settle down onto one curve is what it means for the sequence of approximations to converge to the solution.
Two pieces of BASIC are new here. LINE (t, y)-(t + deltat, y + deltay), j has a fourth argument, a color number, so approximation number j is drawn in color j. COLOR 8, 7 sets the foreground to color 8 (dark gray) and the background to color 7 (light gray). (SCREEN 9 switches to an older color graphics mode.) One quirk of the original carries over: approximation 7 is drawn in color 7, the same light gray as the background, so it is invisible. Try changing the background in color(8, 7) to 15 (white) or 0 (black) to see it.
In the Python, line(..., j) and color(8, 7) do the same jobs, using the same sixteen color numbers as QBasic; the legend under the graph shows which color goes with which approximation and how many segments it has. BASIC’s ^ for powers is ** in Python. Try changing range(1, 15) to range(1, 6) to see just the first few approximations, or change tfinal and the window to look at the long-run behavior.

title: A sequence of approximations: nested loops and color
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  SCREEN 9
 3  COLOR 8, 7
 4  WINDOW (0, 0)-(75, 1300)
 5  FOR j = 1 TO 14
 6          tinitial = 0
 7          tfinal = 75
 8          t = tinitial
 9          y = 100
10          numberofsteps = 2 ^ (j - 1)
11          deltat = (tfinal - tinitial) / numberofsteps
12          FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
13                  yprime = .1 * y * (1 - y / 1000)
14                  deltay = yprime * deltat
15                  LINE (t, y)-(t + deltat, y + deltay), j
16                  t = t + deltat
17                  y = y + deltay
18          NEXT k
19  NEXT j

title: Graphing an accumulation function
text:
← PreviousAccumulation: a table of valuesAll appsNext →Newton's method
This page runs a BASIC program that graphs the accumulation function
\[
A(t) = \int_0^t \cos(s^2)\, ds
\]
from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 4\). The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The calculation is the same as in TABLE, now with 400 steps instead of 8, and instead of printing each value the program draws it. On each step, deltay = fnf(t) * deltat is how much the accumulation changes, and LINE (t, accumulation)-(t + deltat, accumulation + deltay) draws a segment from the current point to the next one. So the slope of each segment is fnf(t), the rate \(\cos(t^2)\). WINDOW (0, 0)-(4, 2) sets t from 0 to 4 across and the accumulation from 0 to 2 up.
Look at the shape: the graph rises steeply at first, where \(\cos(t^2)\) is near 1, reaches a high point near \(t \approx 1.25\) (where \(t^2 = \pi/2\) and the rate turns negative), and then wiggles faster and faster as \(\cos(t^2)\) oscillates more and more quickly, settling down around 0.6. Try numberofsteps = 8 to see the rough version from TABLE drawn as a graph, or change fnf to graph a different accumulation.
QBasic lets a FUNCTION be written at the end of the program, after the code that uses it. Python needs a function to be defined before it is called, so in the Python the def comes first, and return gives back the value that BASIC sets with fnf = .... COS becomes math.cos, and ^ becomes **.

title: Graphing an accumulation function
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  SCREEN 12
 3  WINDOW (0, 0)-(4, 2)
 4  tinitial = 0
 5  tfinal = 4
 6  t = tinitial
 7  accumulation = 0
 8  numberofsteps = 400
 9  deltat = (tfinal - tinitial) / numberofsteps
10  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
11          deltay = fnf(t) * deltat
12          LINE (t, accumulation)-(t + deltat, accumulation + deltay)
13          accumulation = accumulation + deltay
14          t = t + deltat
15  NEXT k
16  FUNCTION fnf (t)
17          fnf = COS(t ^ 2)
18  END FUNCTION

title: Newton’s method
text:
← PreviousGraphing an accumulation functionAll appsNext →Riemann sums
This page runs a BASIC program that uses Newton’s method to solve
\[
g(x) = 4x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0.
\]
The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to run it again; Reset brings back the original program.
Starting from a guess, Newton’s method follows the tangent line to the graph of g down to the x-axis and takes the place where it crosses as the next guess:
\[
x_{\text{new}} = x - \frac{g(x)}{g'(x)}.
\]
In the program, g is the value of the function, gprime is its derivative \(12x^2 + 6x + 2\), and x = x - g / gprime is the Newton step. Each line of output shows the step number n and the current guess x, starting from start = -1. By step 6 the guess has settled at \(-0.605829586188268\), and the remaining steps don’t change it. As with the Babylonian method, the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each step once the guess is close.
Try other values of start. Since \(g'(x) = 12x^2 + 6x + 2\) is never zero, this cubic has only one root, so every start leads to the same answer, though some take longer. Try changing g and gprime to solve a different equation; just be sure gprime really is the derivative of g, or the method will wander.
Note that the loop runs FOR n = 0 TO numberofsteps, which is 9 passes, starting at 0; in Python that is range(0, numberofsteps + 1). BASIC’s ^ becomes **.

title: Newton’s method
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  start = -1
 3  numberofsteps = 8
 4  x = start
 5  FOR n = 0 TO numberofsteps
 6          PRINT n, x
 7          g = 4 * x ^ 3 + 3 * x ^ 2 + 2 * x + 1
 8          gprime = 12 * x ^ 2 + 6 * x + 2
 9          x = x - g / gprime
10  NEXT n

title: Accumulation: a table of values
text:
← PreviousThe Babylonian method for square rootsAll appsNext →Graphing an accumulation function
This page runs a BASIC program that makes a table for the accumulation function
\[
A(t) = \int_0^t \cos(s^2)\, ds,
\]
the solution of \(y' = \cos(t^2)\) with \(y(0) = 0\). The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to run it again; Reset brings back the original program.
There is no formula for \(A(t)\) in terms of familiar functions, but Euler’s method doesn’t need one. The interval from 0 to 4 is split into numberofsteps pieces of width deltat. On each piece the program computes deltay = fnf(t) * deltat, the rate at the start of the step times the width, adds it to accumulation, and moves t ahead. Each line of output shows three numbers: deltay, the running total accumulation, and the new value of t. Watch deltay change sign as \(\cos(t^2)\) swings between positive and negative; when it is negative, the accumulation goes down.
With only \(2^3 = 8\) steps the table is rough. Change numberofsteps to 2 ** 6 or 2 ** 10 and compare the last value of accumulation with the 1.1330 you get here.
QBasic lets a FUNCTION be written at the end of the program, after the code that uses it. Python needs a function to be defined before it is called, so in the Python the def comes first, and return gives back the value that BASIC sets with fnf = .... COS becomes math.cos, and ^ becomes **.

text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program

 2  tinitial = 0
 3  tfinal = 4
 4  t = tinitial
 5  numberofsteps = 2 ^ 3
 6  deltat = (tfinal - tinitial) / numberofsteps
 7  accumulation = 0
 8  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
 9          deltay = fnf(t) * deltat
10          accumulation = accumulation + deltay
11          t = t + deltat
12          PRINT deltay, accumulation, t
13  NEXT k
14  FUNCTION fnf (t)
15          fnf = COS(t ^ 2)
16  END FUNCTION

title: Arc length: adding up short segments
text:
← PreviousA sequence of approximations: nested loops and colorAll appsNext →The Babylonian method for square roots
This page runs a BASIC program that estimates the length of a curve, the parabola \(y = x^2\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 1\). The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to run it again; Reset brings back the original program.
The idea is to replace the curve by \(n\) straight segments that join points on it. The loop finds the two ends of segment k, at xl and xr, and uses the Pythagorean theorem to get its length:
\[
\text{segment} = \sqrt{(x_r - x_l)^2 + (y_l - y_r)^2}.
\]
Each pass adds that length to total and prints k and the segment’s length; at the end the program prints n and the total. With n = 2 the estimate is about 1.4604. The true length is about 1.4789, and the chain of segments always comes out a little shorter than the curve, because a straight segment is the shortest path between its ends. Try n = 10, 100, and 1000 to watch the total close in on 1.4789, or change fnf to measure a different curve.
A few BASIC habits translate differently. QBasic lets a FUNCTION be written at the end of the program, after the code that uses it. Python needs a function to be defined before it is called, so in the Python the def comes first, and return gives back the value that BASIC sets with fnf = .... SQR is BASIC’s square root; in Python it is math.sqrt, which needs import math at the top. BASIC’s ^ for powers is ** in Python. Finally, QBasic quietly starts every variable at 0, so the original never sets total = 0; Python stops with an error if a variable is used before it has a value, so the Python sets it before the loop.

title: Arc length: adding up short segments
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  xinitial = 0
 3  xfinal = 1
 4  n = 2
 5  deltax = (xfinal - xinitial) / n
 6  FOR k = 1 TO n
 7          xl = xinitial + (k - 1) * deltax
 8          xr = xinitial + k * deltax
 9          yl = fnf(xl)
10          yr = fnf(xr)
11          segment = SQR((xr - xl) ^ 2 + (yl - yr) ^ 2)
12          total = total + segment
13          PRINT k, segment
14  NEXT k
15  PRINT n, total
16  FUNCTION fnf (x)
17          fnf = x ^ 2
18  END FUNCTION

title: The Babylonian method for square roots
text:
← PreviousArc length: adding up short segmentsAll appsNext →Accumulation: a table of values
This page runs a BASIC program that finds \(\sqrt{5}\) using a method known to the Babylonians nearly 4,000 years ago. The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to run it again; Reset brings back the original program.
Start with a guess, x = 2. If x is too small, then 5/x is too large, and the other way around, so the true square root lies between them. Their average,
\[
x_{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x + \frac{a}{x}\right),
\]
is a better guess. The loop does this n = 6 times and prints each new guess. The guesses are 2.25, then 2.2361111…, then 2.2360679779…, and from the fourth step on the printed value no longer changes: 2.23606797749979 is \(\sqrt{5}\) to every digit the computer keeps. Notice how fast this is. Roughly, the number of correct digits doubles with each step. (Later in the course this turns out to be Newton’s method applied to \(x^2 - a = 0\).)
Try other values of a, a bad starting guess such as x = 100, or x = -2 to see which square root you end up with. Nothing in this program needs anything special in Python; only FOR k = 1 TO n becomes for k in range(1, n + 1):.

title: The Babylonian method for square roots
text:
Notes from the textbook

 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  a = 5
 3  x = 2
 4  n = 6
 5  FOR k = 1 TO n
 6          x = (x + a / x) / 2
 7          PRINT x
 8  NEXT k

title: Riemann sums
text:
← PreviousNewton's methodAll appsNext →Graphing a Taylor polynomial
This page runs a BASIC program that computes a Riemann sum for
\[
\int_1^3 \sqrt{1 + x^3}\, dx.
\]
The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to run it again; Reset brings back the original program.
The interval from a = 1 to b = 3 is split into numberofsteps pieces of width deltax. On each piece, deltaS = fnf(x) * deltax is the area of a rectangle whose height is the value of the function at the left end of the piece. The program adds these up in accumulation and prints each rectangle’s area next to the running total. With 4 steps the sum is about 5.2916.
This integral has no formula in terms of familiar functions, so the Riemann sum is the way to find its value, which is about 6.22996. Because \(\sqrt{1 + x^3}\) is increasing on \([1, 3]\), each left-endpoint rectangle sits below the curve and the sum comes out too small. Try numberofsteps = 40, 400, and 4000 and watch the last total climb toward 6.22996. (For large values the output gets long; you may want to move the print out of the loop so it prints just the final total.)
QBasic lets a FUNCTION be written at the end of the program, after the code that uses it. Python needs a function to be defined before it is called, so in the Python the def comes first, and return gives back the value that BASIC sets with fnf = .... SQR becomes math.sqrt, and ^ becomes **.

title: Riemann sums
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  a = 1
 3  b = 3
 4  numberofsteps = 4
 5  deltax = (b - a) / numberofsteps
 6  x = a
 7  accumulation = 0
 8  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
 9          deltaS = fnf(x) * deltax
10          accumulation = accumulation + deltaS
11          x = x + deltax
12          PRINT deltaS, accumulation
13  NEXT k
14  FUNCTION fnf (x)
15          fnf = SQR(1 + x ^ 3)
16  END FUNCTION

title: Graphing a Taylor polynomial
text:
← PreviousRiemann sumsAll apps
This page runs a BASIC program that graphs the Taylor polynomial of degree 17 for \(\sin x\),
\[
x - \frac{x^3}{3!} + \frac{x^5}{5!} - \cdots + \frac{x^{17}}{17!},
\]
from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 3.14\). The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The program has two functions. fnfact(m) computes \(m!\) by multiplying 2, 3, …, m together. fnpoly(x) builds the polynomial term by term: it starts the sum at x, then for k = 3, 5, 7, …, 17 adds Sign * x ^ k / fnfact(k), flipping Sign between −1 and +1 each time so the terms alternate. The main loop steps x across the window by 0.01 and draws a segment from \((x, \text{fnpoly}(x))\) to the next point. WINDOW (0, -1.5)-(3.14, 1.5) sets x from 0 to 3.14 across and y from −1.5 to 1.5 up.
On this interval the polynomial is so close to \(\sin x\) that you couldn’t tell them apart. To see where it fails, widen the window and the loop, say to 10 or 12, and lower the 17 in range(3, 18, 2) to get fewer terms. To compare with the real thing, add a second line inside the loop, line((x, math.sin(x)), (x + 0.01, math.sin(x + 0.01)), 4), with import math at the top; the last number draws it in red.
Two things change in Python. QBasic lets a FUNCTION be written at the end of the program, after the code that uses it. Python needs a function to be defined before it is called, so in the Python the def comes first, and return gives back the value that BASIC sets with fnf = .... And BASIC’s FOR x = 0 TO 3.14 STEP .01 counts in steps of 0.01, but Python’s range only counts in whole numbers, so the Python uses a while loop that adds 0.01 to x each time. Likewise FOR k = 3 TO 17 STEP 2 becomes range(3, 18, 2), since range stops just before its second number.

title: Graphing a Taylor polynomial
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  SCREEN 12
 3  WINDOW (0, -1.5)-(3.14, 1.5)
 4  FOR x = 0 TO 3.14 STEP .01
 5          LINE (x, fnpoly(x))-(x + .01, fnpoly(x + .01))
 6  NEXT x
 7  FUNCTION fnfact (m)
 8          P = 1
 9          FOR r = 2 TO m
10                  P = P * r
11          NEXT r
12          fnfact = P
13  END FUNCTION
14  FUNCTION fnpoly (x)
15          Sum = x
16          Sign = -1
17          FOR k = 3 TO 17 STEP 2
18                  Sum = Sum + Sign * x ^ k / fnfact(k)
19                  Sign = (-1) * Sign
20          NEXT k
21          fnpoly = Sum
22  END FUNCTION
